faq.q: What is the meaning of a leap of faith?
faq.a: A leap of faith is a decision to believe in something or act on it without proof that it will work out. It means moving forward once you’ve gathered what information you can and certainty still isn’t available.

faq.q: Who came up with the idea of a leap of faith?
faq.a: The concept is closely associated with the Danish philosopher Søren Kierkegaard, who argued that some deep commitments can’t be reached by reason alone and require a personal choice.

faq.q: Is a leap of faith the same as being reckless?
faq.a: No. A real leap of faith follows careful thought, aligns with your values, and considers the downside. Recklessness skips those steps.

faq.q: How do I know if I’m ready to take a leap of faith?
faq.a: Ask whether you’ve done reasonable research, whether the choice fits your values, whether you could recover from the worst realistic outcome, and whether you’d regret not trying.

faq.q: What does “leap and the net will appear” mean?
faq.a: It’s a popular saying suggesting that support and resources often become visible only after you commit. In practice, the net tends to show up as many small supports rather than one rescue.

faq.q: How can I make a leap of faith less scary?
faq.a: Test the change in small ways first, build a financial or emotional cushion, set a real decision date, and share your plan with someone you trust.
